question: How does H-Net decide where chunk boundaries go?
gold: Routing module: cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs; low similarity -> high boundary probability; first position always a boundary
text:
Evidence: "In order to compute 𝑝𝑡 , we need 𝑘𝑡−1 (see equation (4)), so our state consists of the key value of the most recent token processed." [HNET §2.4 Autoregressive Training and Inference, p.9]
The routing module uses the key of the most recent token to evaluate 𝑝𝑡, effectively deciding whether to start a new chunk at that token . [HNET §2.4 Autoregressive Training and Inference, p.9]
citations: HNET §2.4 Autoregressive Training and Inference, p.9
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "During training, H‑Net employs standard causal masking across all sequence mixing layers. DC maintains causality by computing boundary probabilities based only on current and previous representations."  
Q2 [C1] "In order to compute 𝑝𝑡 , we need 𝑘𝑡−1 (see equation (4)), so our state consists of the key value of the most recent token processed."  
Q3 [C2] "In Figure 4, we provide visualizations of the boundaries dynamically drawn by HNet (1‑stage) and H‑Net (2‑stage). The visualization offers several insights about how the model decides boundaries."  

ANSWER: H‑Net decides chunk boundaries by computing a boundary probability 𝑝𝑡 for each token using only the current and previous representations, ensuring causality [Q1]. The routing module uses the key of the most recent token to evaluate 𝑝𝑡, effectively deciding whether to start a new chunk at that token [Q2]. Visualizations show that the model learns to place boundaries at whitespace or content‑aware positions, dynamically adjusting based on the token sequence [Q3].

question: What is the ratio loss in dynamic chunking and why is it needed?
gold: A loss that guides the fraction of selected boundaries toward a target compression ratio; without it the model could keep everything or compress too much
text:
Evidence: "Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information)." [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
Evidence: "we introduce a ratio loss to guide compression: 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺))" [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
Evidence: "When 𝐹 = 𝐺, the loss attains a minimum of Lratio = 1 when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 ." [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
This prevents trivial solutions where the model either keeps almost everything or compresses too much, ensuring content‑adaptive compression . [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information)."  
Q2 [C1] "we introduce a ratio loss to guide compression: 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺))"  
Q3 [C1] "When 𝐹 = 𝐺, the loss attains a minimum of Lratio = 1 when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 ."

ANSWER: The ratio loss is a regularization term that encourages the model to keep a target compression ratio. It penalizes the difference between the actual fraction of retained vectors (𝐹) and the average boundary probability (𝐺), driving them toward the desired ratio 𝑁1. This prevents trivial solutions where the model either keeps almost everything or compresses too much, ensuring content‑adaptive compression [Q1][Q2][Q3].

question: Why did the authors of Attention Is All You Need choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
gold: Both gave nearly identical results; sinusoidal may let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than seen in training
text:
Evidence: "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
The authors chose sinusoidal encodings because they hypothesize it lets the model learn relative positions via a linear relationship between offsets, and because it may extrapolate to longer sequences . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
They also tested learned embeddings and found similar performance, so the choice was mainly for extrapolation and relative‑position convenience . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ."  
Q2 [C1] "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))."  
Q3 [C1] "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training."  

ANSWER: The authors chose sinusoidal encodings because they hypothesize it lets the model learn relative positions via a linear relationship between offsets, and because it may extrapolate to longer sequences [Q1][Q3]. They also tested learned embeddings and found similar performance, so the choice was mainly for extrapolation and relative‑position convenience [Q2].
